source.title: Joint Edge-Model Sparse Learning is Provably Efficient for Graph Neural Networks
source.authors: Shuai Zhang; M. Wang; Pin-Yu Chen; Sijia Liu; Song-Tao Lu; Miaoyuan Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analytically derives and experimentally evaluates training convergence and zero generalization error for a one-hidden-layer GNN under specified synthetic graph data assumptions. This bears conceptually on gradient training from random initialization, but it does not test the listed CIFAR, depth, initialization, learning-rate, or batch-normalization settings.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own convergence experiments and zero-generalization-error theorem. Citation-only claims about other work and quantities used only to describe theoretical bounds or select settings are not separate results.
record.test_reason: The study's own results concern GNN sparsification, sample complexity and convergence on structured graph data. They do not test any listed version. V1 concerns training classification error in CIFAR convolutional networks; these results concern a different system and chiefly generalization. Width sweeps do not measure V2's teacher-student local-minimum failures, and rewinding comparisons do not test V4's signal-preserving initialization claim. Safran and Shamir's local-minimum result is cited, not independently tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors derive sample-complexity and convergence guarantees for joint graph sampling and magnitude-based neuron pruning in structurally constrained two-layer GNNs, and report supporting synthetic and practical graph experiments. The theoretical benefits require the stated sampling and pruning conditions; they are not guarantees for arbitrary sparsification.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a one-hidden-layer graph neural network with a max-pooling ReLU aggregator, mini-batch SGD, edge sampling, optional neuron magnitude pruning, and rewind. Synthetic-data experiments use full-batch gradient descent; no CIFAR benchmark recipe is tested.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with importance-sampling probability α, pruning rate β, sampled-neighbor count r, hidden width K, feature noise σ, and training sample size. Random pruning performs worse than magnitude pruning in reported synthetic comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: The theory guarantees zero graph-wide margin error under structural-data, width, sample and iteration assumptions. Synthetic experiments relate success and convergence to sampling, pruning, width and noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under specified structured graph-data conditions, randomly initialized shallow max-pooling GNNs can learn correct classifications, with importance sampling and magnitude pruning reducing sample requirements and convergence iterations.

fits_no_version.finding: Joint sparsification improves test performance in reported citation-network and large-scale graph experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Graph sampling and magnitude-based neuron pruning can improve GNN test performance or reduce the labeled samples needed for a given test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 17 reports faster convergence with rewinding than with fresh random initialization after pruning; fresh initialization performs worse than the dense baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reusing the original surviving-neuron initialization can improve convergence of magnitude-pruned GNNs relative to freshly initializing the pruned architecture.

record.code_released: Source code is stated to be in the supplementary material; no URL is stated for that code.
record.problems: The theoretical guarantee relies on structural assumptions and a one-hidden-layer GNN. The synthetic experiments use a constructed graph-data distribution. Real-data experiments report test error, not training classification error. Several numerical results are figure-only, and the paper says it includes only partial real-data results due to space limits.
record.rows_left_out: No results left out for the 60-row limit. Citation-only results and theoretical quantities used only to motivate or set the method are not rows.

untested.parts: CIFAR convolutional-network training classification error, including random labels and size, stopping or regularization comparisons.
Teacher-student spurious-local-minimum frequencies and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts or the specified alternative recipes.
Activation-matched signal and gradient preservation, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss transients, curvature evolution and divergence.
Batch normalization's training-speed and learning-rate benefits, and comparison with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to the listed claim versions, not denials of the paper's reported effects. Different outcomes and settings are untested parts, not limits_scope verdicts. No additional result bearing on V1–V6 requires a missing entry.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, or small-model and early-stopping comparisons. The theorem addresses zero generalization error in its stated synthetic structural-data setup, not training classification error on image benchmarks.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer GNN (Algorithm 1)

rows.stage_stated: random initialization; pre-training, pruning, rewind, and re-training
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 1 gives conditions under which mini-batch SGD with edge sampling and optional magnitude pruning achieves zero generalization error.

conditions.value: structural graph data with bounded noise σ < 1/L and assumptions (A1), (A2)
class-relevant neighbor sampling probability lower bound α

rows.note: The theorem states zero generalization error for the model under its sample, iteration, width, noise, and data assumptions; this is not a CIFAR training-error measurement.
rows.check: A conditional theoretical guarantee for a max-pooling GNN, not an observed CIFAR training-error result. Equation (3) averages over all graph nodes, including training nodes, so the theorem also implies correct training-node classification under its assumptions; the system and setting still fall outside V1.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The theorem states zero generalization error with probability at least 1 − q^−10 under its sample, width, noise, pruning, and iteration conditions (R1).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The reported experiments reach zero test/generalization error under the defined success criterion and show success or convergence improving with importance sampling and magnitude pruning (R2–R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Reported real-data outcomes measure test error/generalization, not training classification error; the experiments also use graph neural networks rather than CIFAR convolutional networks (R9–R12).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Sample complexity rises with r^2 in the reported sweep, qualifying any broad claim that more sampling or graph sparsification uniformly reduces sample needs (R13).
